historical_spelling: sar, sare, sarre, sær, sore, zore, soir, sair
job: intensifier: severely, greatly, painfully (adverb); painful, grievous, severe (adjective)
definition: Adverb: so as to cause considerable physical pain or injury; severely, grievously; greatly, deeply (OED sore adv.). Adjective: causing or involving pain or distress; in intensive use very great or serious (OED sore adj.1).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED): after a verb of striking or hurting, OE-ModE: OE "Þonne he hi sare sloh" (Anglo-Saxon Psalter lxxvii. 33); after a verb of grieving, OE-ModE: OE "Me þæt cynn hafað sare abolgen." (Genesis 1257); before a participle or adjective of distress, ME-ModE: c1175 "sare offdredde" (Ormulum l. 3809); full sore, ME-EME: c1320 "Fulle sore mowe heo then dreden." (Castle of Love 1580); comparative and superlative, ME-ModE: 1340 "Huo þet heȝest ualþ þe zorer he him blecheþ." (Ayenbite 238); to sit one sore, ME-EME (obsolete c1420-1560): c1420 "That sittus me nowe fulle sore." (Sir Amadace xxi); lay sore upon, EME: 1611 "because shee lay sore vpon him" (KJV Judges xiv. 17; only quotation found); before a noun, OE-ModE: OE "Nu þu ealle forlæt sare sorgceare." (Crist I 209); latest 1892 "a sore temptation" (Photography Annual vol. II. 893). Now chiefly archaic and dialect.

job: perfect tense of an intransitive verb, formed with be and the past participle, expressing the state reached
definition: In intransitive verbs, forming tenses of the perfect; in later use chiefly with verbs of motion such as come, go, rise, set, fall, arrive, depart, grow, etc., expressing a condition or state attained at the time of speaking, rather than the action of reaching it, e.g. ‘the sun is set’, ‘our guests are gone’, ‘Babylon is fallen’, ‘the children are all grown up’. Now largely replaced by have following the pattern of transitive verbs (OED be v., sense IV.16.b).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED be v., IV.16.b): be + past participle of an intransitive verb, OE-ModE: OE "Min broðer is faren of þisse liue." (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, MS Laud, Peterborough interpolation, anno 656); ME "Þe grete lordes..beþ lenged now here." (William of Palerne l. 1457, a1375); ME "In euell tyme ben oure enmyes entred." (Merlin 165, a1500); EME "These children, Which accidentally are met together." (Shakespeare, Comedy of Errors v. i. 353, a1616); EME "Therefore I am return'd." (Milton, Paradise Regain'd ii. 140, 1671); ModE "His parents were grown old." (C. M. Yonge, Cameos 1st Series ix. 58, 1868); latest "The..purple lupine blossoms are gone forever." (J. R. Smith, San Francisco's Lost Landmarks, 2005).

date: eOE (Charter: Lufu to Christ Church, Canterbury, Sawyer 1197)
job: perfect tenses formed with have and the past participle (present perfect, past perfect, perfect infinitive)
definition: As an auxiliary verb used with the past participle of another verb, forming the present perfect (OED have v., VI.i), the past perfect (VI.ii) and the perfect infinitive (VI.iii.36). With an intransitive verb denoting a change from one state or position to another, as come, depart, go, grow, etc., cf. be v. IV.16b (OED have v., VI.i.31.c).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED have v., VI): present perfect with a transitive verb, OE: OE "Þin geleafa hæfð þe gehæled" (Ælfric, Catholic Homilies: 1st Series x. 258); present perfect with an intransitive verb of change of state or position (VI.i.31.c), ME-ModE: a1225 "He munegede alle þa þet þo weren oðer seoþðen habbeð ikumen..to endeles blisse." (MS Lambeth in R. Morris, Old English Homilies 1st Series 145); ?a1425 (c1400) "After this I haue gon toward the parties meridionales, þat is, toward the south." (Mandeville's Travels, MS Titus C.xvi, p. 120); 1703 "Many of our English Valetudinarians have gone from Jamaica..to the I. Caimanes." (W. Dampier, Voyage to New Holland ii. 81); 1768 "I have come laughing all the way from London to Paris." (L. Sterne, Sentimental Journey vol. II. 63); past perfect with an intransitive verb of change of position (VI.ii.34.b), OE and EME: OE "Hie ða beahhrodene feðelaste forð onettan, oð hie glædmode gegan hæfdon to ðam wealgate." (Judith 140); 1651 "I wish from my hart Mr. Attorney had come away." (in E. Nicholas, Papers vol. I. 249); perfect infinitive after a modal (VI.iii.36.a), EME-ModE: a1616 "I should haue lost the worth of it in Gold." (Shakespeare, Cymbeline ii. iv. 42); 1796 "Hours might have passed, unnumbered and unawares." (F. Burney, Camilla vol. V. x. xiii. 531); 1876 "I might have been abashed by their authority." (W. E. Gladstone, Homeric Synchronism 72).
quote: Ðet ic beboden hebbe an ðisem gewrite.

historical_spelling: vnderwode, vnderwod, Underwode, vnderwood, Vnder-wood, Under-wood, vnderwoodes
date: a1325 (Statutes of the Realm, MS Rawlinson B.520)
job: woody growth beneath timber: small trees, shrubs, coppice-wood or brushwood (noun)
definition: Small trees or shrubs, coppice-wood or brush-wood, growing beneath higher timber trees (OED underwood n., sense 1.a); figuratively (1.b); with a and plural, a quantity or stretch, a special kind, of woody undergrowth (sense 2).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED underwood n.): sense 1.a, woody growth beneath timber, ME-LMdE: ME a1325 "Þat te heiwes [= highways]..ben..ilargiste þerase is wode, hegges, oþer buskes, ore vnderwode." (Statutes of Realm, MS Rawlinson B.520, xiii. 68); ME c1380 "His taile is likenyd to a cedre, [þat] wexyng in to heȝþe passiþ oþer vnderwod." (Antecrist in J. H. Todd, Three Treat. Wycklyffe 119); ME 1467-8 "Every persone or persones, which have bought eny Tymbre, Woode or Underwode." (Rolls of Parliament V. 575/2); ME 1480 "The people..throwen down & beren away the vnderwode of þe seid Priour." (Coventry Leet Book 445); EMdE 1512 "Underwode growyng uppon the seid landes." (Act 4 Henry VIII c. 18 §17); EMdE a1596 "Thinke when an oake fals, vnderwood shrinkes downe, And yet may liue, though brusd." (Sir Thomas More, 1911, Add. i. 65); EMdE 1642 "This underwood serves for supplies to save timber from burning." (T. Fuller, Holy State ii. xiii. 100); EMdE 1669 "In a few years you may observe many fair Trees to steal up amongst the Under-wood." (J. Worlidge, Systema Agriculturæ, 1681, 93); LMdE 1733 "The Underwood will be fit to fell in..fifteen Years." (W. Ellis, Chiltern & Vale Farming 128); LMdE 1794 "At a deep recess of the forest..so overgrown with underwood, that they proceeded with difficulty." (A. Radcliffe, Mysteries of Udolpho IV. vi. 117); LMdE 1827 "Our way..was nearly free from underwood or any material impediment." (O. W. Roberts, Narrative of Voyages Central America 64); latest LMdE 1882 "She made her way through the dense underwood." ('Ouida', In Maremma I. 46). Sense 1.b, figurative, EMdE-LMdE: a1637 "So am I bold to entitle these lesser Poems, of later growth, by this [name] of Vnder-wood" (B. Jonson, Under-woods To Reader, Workes 1640, III); 1693 "But these are the Under-wood of Satire, rather than the Timber-Trees." (J. Dryden, Discourse conc. Satire); 1863 "It is from among the underwood of these stately productions..that we bring to remembrance gems of practical wisdom." (C. Cowden Clarke, Shakespeare-characters ix. 230). Sense 2, with a and plural, a stretch or kind of woody undergrowth, EMdE-LMdE: 1541 "All woodes and vnderwoodes, belonging to your office." (Act 33 Henry VIII c. 39); 1581-2 "Breers, brembles, bushes and underwoodes." (Catal. Anc. Deeds V. 484); 1607 "Therefore must the Surueyor be heedful..to note what trees are among the underwoods." (J. Norden, Surueyors Dialogue iii. 140); 1646 "Great Oakes breake their own branches and neighbouring underwoods." (J. Hall, Horæ Vacivæ 101); 1708 "Posting the..Granadiers among the Thickets of an Underwood." (London Gazette No. 4475/3). OED has no Old English attestation (earliest evidence is before 1325). Formed in English from under- + wood (OED etymology). OED frequency: about 0.1 occurrences per million words in modern written English; no quotation later than 1882 in the entry.

historical_spelling: weardian, wærdedon, weardode, weardiað, wardi, wardiden, warde, warden, warded, warding, ward, weard, uard, warde, wardes
job: to guard, defend or keep safe, and to keep a threat off (verb); a keeper or guard (noun)
definition: Verb: to guard, stand guard over; to keep in safety, take care of; to defend, protect (OED ward v.1, sense 1.a); to defend or protect from (1.b); to avert, keep off harm or danger (7); intransitive, to take up a position of defence, take precautions against (8, obsolete). Noun: a watchman, guard, keeper, warden (OED ward n.1, obsolete, Old English to 1473).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED ward v.1 and ward n.1): VERB sense 1.a, to guard or keep safe with a direct object, OE-LMdE: OE "Þa Englisce men þe wærdedon þære sæ." (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, MS Laud, annal 1087); ME (c1384) "Thei goynge forth, kepten, or wardiden, the sepulcre." (Wycliffite Bible, Early Version, Matthew xxvii. 66); EMdE 1597 "Then if you fight against Gods enemie, God will in iustice, ward you as his souldiers." (Shakespeare, Richard III v. v. 208); LMdE 1893 "Hope Park, a beautiful pleasance..warded by a keeper." (R. L. Stevenson, Catriona viii. 87); latest 1913 "Your wits must ward your head." (Blackwood's Magazine, December 787/1). Sense 1.b, to defend or protect from, ?c1225-1850: ?c1225 "Biseched ȝeorne god..þet he wite & wardi ow wið alle þet ou weited." (Ancrene Riwle, MS Cleopatra C.vi, 134); EMdE 1565 "The other two [angels] warding him on eche side from the danger of the fire also." (T. Stapleton, trans. Bede); EMdE 1594 "Tell him it was a hand that warded him From thousand dangers." (Shakespeare, Titus Andronicus ii. i. 193); EMdE 1604 "Abraham..was constrayned to warde his offring from the molestfull crowes." (T. Wright, Passions of Minde vi. 318); LMdE 1850 "Loxias himself will ward His holiest shrine from lawless outrage." (J. S. Blackie, trans. Aeschylus). Sense 1.d, intransitive, to keep guard, ME-LMdE: 1390 "And in this hous to loke and warde Was Minotaurus put in warde." (Gower, Confessio Amantis); 1722 "The Family..left the..Fellows warding, and watching." (Defoe, Journal of the Plague Year 63). Sense 2, to rule or act as guardian, OE-1400: OE "Nabochodonossor.. weardode wide rice." (Caedmon's Dan. 665); 1390 "tok this child into his warde, And seide he wolde him kepe and warde." (Gower, Confessio Amantis I. 345). Sense 7, to avert or keep off harm, a1586-: a1586 "While they did ward sun-beames with shady bay." (Sir P. Sidney, Arcadia); 1810 "I, only I, can ward their fate." (W. Scott, The Lady of the Lake v. 220); with off (7.b) 1759 "If then you would ward off the gripe of poverty, pretend to be a stranger to her." (O. Goldsmith, Bee). Sense 8, intransitive, to take precautions against (obsolete, 1230-1753): 1709 "To ward against the coming Blow." (M. Prior, Paulo Purganti 100); 1726 "Regard must be had..in cold Countries to ward against the bleak Northwind." (G. Leoni, trans. L. B. Alberti, Architecture I. 99); 1745 "In England, this pusillanimity is more to be warded against than in most other countries." (J. Swift). Sense 1.c, figurative, to guard a secret, 1881: "obliges me to ward a secret." (A. J. Duffield, trans. Cervantes, Don Quixote II. 442). NOUN ward n.1, a watchman, guard, keeper, warden (obsolete, OE-1473): OE "Nu scylun hergan hefaen-ricaes uard." (Caedmon, Hymn 1); OE "Weard Scildinga, se þe holmclifu healdan scolde." (Beowulf 229); 1377 "For any wye or warde wide opene the ȝatis." (W. Langland, Piers Plowman B. xviii. 320); ?1473 "Thou hast slayn the wardes of the serpentes and the portyers of the lyons" (W. Caxton, trans. R. Le Fevre, Recuyell of Histroyes of Troye, 1894, I. ii. 106). The OED says the noun was later used chiefly as the second element in compounds, as bear-, gate-, hay-, mill-, woodward. OED frequency of the verb: about 2 occurrences per million words in modern written English. The OED pages supplied have no quotation of the verb after 1913 and none of the noun after ?1473, so no PDE use is shown here. The OED pages for ward v.2, ward n.2, and the list of compounds and derived words were not supplied, so a warding adjective, a warding gerund and the compound fyrward are not covered.

job: the duty, office or state of guarding; guardianship of a minor
definition: The office or position of guardian: the guardianship of a minor, in Feudal Law the guardianship and custody of the person and lands of a minor with all profits accruing during his or her minority (OED wardship n., sense 1.a); guardianship, protection, custody, chiefly figurative (1.b); the state or condition of being a ward (2.a); transferred and figurative (2.b).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED wardship n.): sense 1.a, the guardianship of a minor, in Feudal Law the guardianship and custody of the person and lands of a minor, ME-LMdE: ME 1454 "Ser, forasmyche as the Kyng hathe grauntyd be hese letteres patentys the wardship wyth the profitys of the londys of T. Fastolf duryng hese noun-age to you and T. H. [etc.]." (J. Russe in Paston Letters & Papers, 2004, II. 104); EMdE 1540 "Personnes, to whom the kinges highnes shall graunt the custodye and wardeship of any of his graces wardes." (Act 32 Henry VIII c. 46); EMdE 1586 "The Master of Glames and the Secretarye have gotten of the King the wardshippe and marriage of the Erle Mongomeris sonne, being but two yeares of age." (T. Randolph); EMdE 1641 "He gave him two rich wardships." (Earl of Monmouth, trans. Biondi); LMdE 1766 "The lord was intitled to the wardship of the heir; and was called the guardian in chivalry." (W. Blackstone, Commentaries II. v. 67); LMdE 1884 "Sect. 35..assigns to the Chancery Division the wardship of infants." (Law Times 77. 309/1). Sense 1.b, general guardianship, protection, custody, chiefly figurative, 1631-: 1631 "[He] freed this kingdome from the wardship of the Peeres." (J. Weever, Ancient Funerall Monuments 456); 1635 "Thou grand Impostor, how hast thou obtain'd The wardship of the world!" (F. Quarles, Emblemes ii. iii. 74); 1765 "..when the earls gave up the wardship of the county." (W. Blackstone, Commentaries I. ix. 335); 1884 "She was already committed to wardship and protection of an empire such as the world had never yet seen." (Lord Rosebery in Pall Mall Gazette); latest 1887 "I try in these my last days to put my memory under wardship." (H. Caine, Deemster III. xxvii. 140). Sense 2.a, the state of being a ward, 1549-: 1549 "Assone as we came out of wardeship, and wer growen vp to a ryper age." (M. Coverdale et al., trans. Erasmus); 1583 "The manis not out of wardshippe by our lawe till xxj. yere olde" (Sir T. Smith, De Republica Anglorum iii. v. 98); 1874 "Three English earls who were in royal wardship were wedded by the King to foreigners." (J. R. Green, Short History of the English People iii. §5. 140). Sense 2.b, transferred and figurative, 1583-: 1800 "I must perforce Leave him in wardship to his innocence." (S. T. Coleridge, trans. Schiller, Piccolomini i. iii. 112); 1876 "We have written the origin of our country; we are now to pursue the history of its wardship." (G. Bancroft). Spellings in the quotations: wardship, wardeship, wardshyp, wardshippe. Formed in English from ward n.2 + -ship (OED etymology). No Old English evidence; earliest use is 1454. OED frequency: about 0.2 occurrences per million words in modern written English. The OED pages supplied have no quotation after 1887, so no PDE use is shown here.

historical_spelling: wardein, wardeyn, wardayn, wardain, wardane, wardens, warden, wardened
job: the guardian or keeper, used as a title (noun); to watch over as a warden (verb)
definition: Noun: one who guards, protects, or defends; occasionally a guardian angel (OED warden n.1, sense 1.a, obsolete); one who has the care of something specified, a keeper (2.a, obsolete except poetic); and many offices from the guardian of an heir to the head of a college or an air-raid warden. Verb: to watch over or guard as a warden (OED warden v., from 1910).
usage_notes: Patterns (OED warden n.1 and warden v.): NOUN sense 1.a, one who guards, protects, or defends; occasionally a guardian angel (obsolete, ?c1225-1513): ?c1225 "Wat crist ure vchan. to swa gentil wardein bereð to lute menske." (Ancrene Riwle, MS Cleopatra C.vi, 232); c1290 "Þere in seint Iohanes warde is swete moder he tok,..hire wardein he was aftur also þat he to heouene i-wende." (John 31 in S.E. Leg. 403); c1400 "There is none so caitif pilgrym that he ne hath assigned hym a wardeyne the hour of his byrthe." (Pylgr. Sowle i. vii.). Sense 2.a, one who has the care of something specified; a keeper (obsolete except poetic, a1290-): a1290 "Þe hayward nom and bleu his horn, For he wes wardein of þat corn." (S. Eustace 230); 1362 "For Rihtfoliche Resoun schulde rulen ou alle, And kuynde wit be wardeyn oure weolþe to kepe." (W. Langland, Piers Plowman A. i. 53); a1400 "Garners and granges fild wit sede,..In ilk sted a sere wardain." (Cursor Mundi, MS Vespasian, 4691); 1871 "Of all this wealth I have made thee warden." (D. G. Rossetti, Eden Bower, Poems xxi). Sense 3, guardian of the person and lands of an orphan heir (obsolete, c1290-1700): 1385 "Thus here wardeynys wolde they disceyue." (G. Chaucer, Legend of Good Women 753); 1579 "Wardeine most properly is he that hath the wardship or keeping of an heire" (Rastell, Exposition Termes of Lawes 97b). Sense 4.a, regent or viceroy (obsolete except historical, a1400-); 4.b, governor of a town, province or district, Warden of the Marches (1297-1917): 1470-85 "And sire Brastias was maade wardeyn to wayte vpon the northe fro Trent forwardes." (T. Malory, Morte d'Arthur i. viii. 44). Sense 5, a guild officer, 1389-: 1640 "Next year wee will haue him warden Of our societie." (P. Massinger, Parliament of Love iv. ii. 57). Sense 6.a, the person having the direction or oversight of some work or enterprise (obsolete, 1398-1601): 1601 "Pythagoras, a great maister and warden of these exercises." (P. Holland, trans. Pliny). Sense 2.d, a gatekeeper, porter, sentinel, now rare, a1250-: 1801 "Fit warden of the sorcery-gate" (R. Southey, Thalaba II. xii. 314); 1894 "Female wardens made a fit outpost for this palace of many women." (R. L. Stevenson, In the South Seas iv. iii. 319). Sense 8.a, custodian of a building, esp. a temple or church (obsolete, 1290-1642): 1642 "The good Herald..is a Warden of the temple of Honour." (T. Fuller, Holy State ii. xxii. 141). Sense 11, head of a college, school or hospital, 1575-: 1855 "..a fitting residence for a warden." (A. Trollope, The Warden i. 3). Sense 12, prison keeper, c1330-: 1330 "Wiþ wardeyns þat hem vndertoke." (R. Mannyng, Chronicle Wace 13112). Sense 7.c, an air-raid warden, 1936-: 1936 "An organization of 'air raid wardens' to give immediate information and to help in dealing with fires caused by incendiary bombs." (Times 11 July 16/4); latest noun quotation 1978 "A tin-hatted Air Raid Warden was hurrying along the street... The Warden hurried on." (E. Malpass, Wind brings up Rain xxvi. 232). Spellings in the quotations: wardein, wardeyn, wardayn, wardain, wardane, warden. VERB warden v., transitive, to watch over or guard as a warden, spec. to watch over or patrol (a nature reserve, etc.), also intransitive to act as a wildlife warden, 1910-: 1910 "To warden the waves was his further bent." (T. Hardy, The Dynasts ii. i. vi. 165); 1971 "Having wardened at the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds reserve at Loch Garten, may I enlarge upon the letter from M. S. M. Burns?" (Times 7 May 17/7); 1974 "It would be wardened and visited regularly to prevent vandalism and litter." (Oxford Times 4 January 7/6); 1982 "The eyres are well wardened against egg collectors." (Lakeland Echo 18 March 5). A borrowing from Old French wardein, north-eastern variant of guarden (OED etymology). The verb is formed within English by conversion from the noun. OED frequency: noun about 2 occurrences per million words; verb about 0.06. No Old English evidence for either. The OED also lists a separate warden n.2 (a baking pear), not used here.
